en: The Profound Mirror of the Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka, Volume One, composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang during the Tang Dynasty.
Having applied myself with deep reflection to this Great Sūtra, I have practiced this contemplation to a modest degree; its essential purport has already been set forth in my commentaries.
Fearing that people might fall into error regarding this profound scripture,
I have briefly extolled these subtle and essential points;
those of sincere devotion may at times further propagate them.
Several of these gentlemen earnestly entreated me to provide an exposition.
They all said that they had been contemplating this matter, visiting friends, and seeking its source;
whether for study or for transmission, they had sought it everywhere among the various exponents of the Śākyamuni teachings.
Doubts and obscurities accumulated over many years have finally been illuminated.
With diligent vigilance throughout the evening, I wish to resolve the profound meaning;
yet, I find myself in the declining years of my life.
Life is as precarious as a candle in the wind;
I fear that subtle contemplation will sink into oblivion and that rambling words will stray from the correct path.
In accordance with this sincere request, I have briefly analyzed the profound and subtle [teachings] and titled it *The Mysterious Mirror of the Dharmadhātu*,
hoping that fellow practitioners of the future will [benefit from it].
I have seen the profound sincerity of the ancient sages.
Guān said: "I shall cultivate the Dharma-gate of the Contemplation of the Dharmadhātu of the Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra."
Briefly, there are three layers.
Shi Fashun of Zhongnan Mountain was surnamed Du.
The commentary states:
The sūtra that serves as the basis for the six characters beginning with "Great" (mahā) omits the word "sūtra.
The contemplation that relies upon it is found below the "Contemplation of the Dharma Realm" (dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā).
Now, first, I shall briefly explain the title of the sutra.
"Mahāvaipulya" refers to the Dharma realized by all Tathāgatas.
The Buddha-Flower Adornment (Buddhāvatamsaka) accords with the Dharma-realm and is that which can realize it.
The Dharma is divided into essence, characteristics, and function.
Human beings possess causes and effects.
That which is "great" is that whose substance is great;
it is the profound realm of reality (dharmadhātu).
It is the essential substance of the minds of all Buddhas and sentient beings.
Vastly encompassing like space, profound and still, eternally abiding, it is conventionally termed "Great.
Thus, a sutra says:
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) pervades all places;
all sentient beings and lands throughout the three periods of time are entirely contained within it without exception,
yet it has no form or characteristic that can be apprehended.
This is precisely the Great Meaning (mahārtha).
As for "Vast" (vaipulya):
its characteristics and functions are all-pervasive; this is the characteristic of the essence itself.
The dharma of the marks and virtues is boundless, which is precisely the function of the marks;
its karmic activity is vast and inexhaustible.
Within the three non-obstructions, the mention of any one fully encompasses all.
The object of noble wisdom is the dharma-dhātu, which is that which is realized.
A Buddha is the fruition,
in which all virtues are perfectly luminous.
The flower is a metaphor for the cause;
the various practices are its radiant splendor,
adorning both the subject and the object.
There are two aspects:
first, the cause of the flower, which is that which is able to adorn; second, the fruit of the Buddha, which is that which is adorned.
By means of the ten perfections as causes, one accomplishes the fruit of the ten bodies;
there is no practice that is not complete,
and no virtue that is not perfected.
The two flowers are that which performs the adornment;
the Mahāvaipulya is that which is adorned.
This essence of adornment—its substance, characteristics, and function—constitutes the three virtues of Buddhahood.
Adorning according to the essence reveals the quality of true permanence;
adorning according to the characteristics distinguishes the quality of accomplished cultivation;
and adorning through the application of cultivation realizes the quality of great function.
It is the Flower Adornment that universally adorns the boundless virtues accomplished by such virtues as they truly are.
Thus, the single general title encompasses essence, characteristics, and function;
and for persons, it includes cause and fruit.
Both the person and the dharma are presented as titles; both the dharma and the metaphor are raised together.
Throughout the three great periods of the sutra, it is entirely Mahāvaipulya.
The five cycles of cause and effect, together with the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*,
each have seven characters in their titles, and each character possesses ten meanings.
I shall now provide a brief explanation.
Regarding the ten meanings of "Great," all seven characters are "great.
The first "great" is the greatness of essence (*tattva-mahat*).
Because the Dharma-realm is eternally pervasive;
the second aspect is its "greatness of characteristics," because the virtues of its nature are boundless.
Third, "vastness" refers to the greatness of function;
because it accords with the essence, its function is all-pervasive.
Fourth, "Buddha" refers to the greatness of the fruit.
This is because the ten bodies all pervade the Dharma-realm.
As for the five flowers, they are "great causes" because the essential nature of Samantabhadra’s practices and vows is omnipresent.
Sixth, "ornamentation" refers to the greatness of wisdom,
because the Buddha’s wisdom is like space and can serve as an ornament. Seventh,
"sūtra" refers to the greatness of the teaching.
This is because even if one were to exhaust the ink of the oceans, one could not write down a single phrase [of its meaning].
Eighth is the greatness of the meaning (*artha-mahattva*):
for all that is realized by these six characters accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Ninth is the greatness of the object (*ālambana-mahattva*):
because these seven characters collectively take all sentient beings as their focal object.
Tenth is the greatness of the activity (*karma-mahattva*).
Because this teaching’s intent extends horizontally and exhausts vertically without ceasing,
and because it possesses ten inexhaustible qualities, it is called "Great.
As for the ten meanings of Vaipulya (Extensive):
The characteristics of the essence correspond to the functions of the essence;
this is precisely the tenfold great function of the ten directions.
As for the ten meanings of the Buddha:
The first greatness is the Dharma-body.
The Buddha takes the Dharma as his body because the Buddha-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
The second aspect is twofold:
because the wisdom-body (jñānakāya) accords with the nature of reality (dharmatā).
The third aspect is expansive.
It is endowed with two bodies:
first, the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body),
because a single body universally pervades as the infinite.
The second is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*),
so called because it can manifest as one or many at will and is omnipresent.
The Buddha encompasses five or six types of bodies.
First is the body of enlightenment (*bodhi-kāya*),
because it is accomplished through the path at the tree of awakening.
Second is the body of majestic power (*vibhūti-kāya*).
Because it first attained perfect enlightenment while illuminating the Bodhisattvas,
the "flower" contains seven or eight bodies.
Seventh is the body of merit.
Because the causes for the manifold merits practiced throughout the three periods of time are as inexhaustible as a great ocean.
Eighth is the body of vows (*praṇidhāna-kāya*).
Because the causes of Vairocana’s vows pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*,
it is "adorned."
The ninth is the body adorned with the marks and signs of excellence.
This is because it is adorned with the marks and signs of excellence within the Lotus Treasury.
As for the sutra:
The tenth power is the sustaining of the body;
because the teaching of the perfect melodic voice is inexhaustible,
even a single sūtra of seven characters results in the attainment of Buddhahood.
Regarding the ten meanings of "Flower Adornment" (Avataṃsaka):
the ten perfections (pāramitās) serve as the flowers that adorn, and the ten bodies (daśakāya) serve as the adornments; because these are not distinct, they constitute the ten adornments.
The scriptural words are omitted;
the ten meanings are likewise abbreviated.
This is the compendium, the integration, the permanence, and the Dharma.
This can be understood accordingly.
The inexhaustible ocean of teachings does not transcend these seven characters;
therefore, one relies upon this teaching to establish the gates of contemplation.
Regarding the statement that "the practice of the Dharma-realm contemplation gate briefly consists of three stages," this is a concise indication of the essential framework.
The single character "practice" (xiu) pervades the entire title of the treatise on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
It refers to the process of perfuming, cultivating, training, and reaching mastery.
What is called the "Dharmadhātu" (Dharma-realm) is the profound essence of this single sutra.
This is because its central tenet is the inconceivable dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of dependent origination.
Now, while the characteristics of the dharma-realm essentially consist of only three aspects,
it generally possesses four types.
First, the dharma-realm of phenomena;
second, the dharma-realm of principle;
third, the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena.
The fourth is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena.
Now, regarding these latter three, their individual phenomena and dharmas are distinct and difficult to describe exhaustively; thus, each specific characteristic of a phenomenon [is examined].
Since all of these can be formed into contemplations (*vipaśyanā*), they are not explained in detail here;
they collectively serve as the essential substratum (*āśraya-bhūta*) for the three contemplations.
These matters consist briefly of ten pairs.
First, doctrine and meaning;
second, principle and phenomena;
third, object and wisdom.
Fourth, the stage of practice;
fifth, cause and effect;
sixth, the primary and secondary [receptacles].
Seventh, essence and function;
eighth, persons and dharmas;
ninth, the inverse and the direct.
Tenth, regarding the responsive manifestations (*saṃdarśana*): each individual event serves as the primary substance (*samyag-mūla*) upon which the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) rely.
[This section also includes] the names of those who composed them, their virtuous conduct, and the causal conditions (*nidāna*).
This is as detailed in his biographies.
Guanding said:
"The Contemplation of True Emptiness is the foremost."
The second is the Contemplation of the Non-obstruction between Principle and Phenomena.
The third is the Contemplation of Universal Interpenetration and Inclusion.
The commentary states:
These three names are listed here:
first, the dharma-dhātu of true emptiness, which corresponds to the original name "principle"; second, the dharma-dhātu of suchness, which corresponds to the original name "suchness";
and third, the dharma-dhātu of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena.
What is called "true emptiness" is not an emptiness of annihilation,
nor is it an emptiness apart from form.
Thus there is clarity within emptiness,
yet even the mark of emptiness is absent;
therefore, it is called true emptiness.
This is as detailed in the text.
Second, regarding the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena:
principle has no form or characteristics, yet it is entirely present within all phenomena.
Because they mutually seize upon one another’s existence and non-existence, they are said to be unimpeded.
This is also as detailed in the full text.
Third, regarding "universal inclusion and containment":
Phenomena are fundamentally obstructive, distinguished by size and other attributes;
principle is fundamentally all-encompassing and pervasive, like space, without obstruction.
By means of principle, phenomena are harmonized so that phenomena are entirely identical with principle.
Even down to a speck of dust or a single hair, all are fully encompassed and pervaded.
When these two are compared with one another, they form ten categories, as explained below.
However, the term *dhātu* (element) refers to the actual phenomena (*vastu*).
The term "dhātu" (element) has the meaning of differentiation; it refers to the boundaries of inexhaustible distinctions.
Therefore, the principle of phenomena is called a "dhātu."
The realm (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "nature" (*prakṛti*).
Because all inexhaustible phenomena share a single nature,
the unobstructed dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) possesses the sense of both "nature" and "portion."
Without destroying the principles of phenomena and reality, there is non-obstruction;
thus, the fourth dharma-realm also possesses these two meanings:
its nature is fused with phenomena.
Each individual phenomenon does not destroy its own characteristic;
for they are mutually interfused according to their nature, in layers upon layers without end.
The commentary says:
The first is the method of the Contemplation of True Emptiness (*zhēnkōng guānfǎ*).
Within it, four propositions and ten gates are briefly established.
The commentary states:
This is the summary heading.
The first two sections each contain four items;
by adding the four items of the third section, there are ten gates in total.
The Contemplation states:
First is the contemplation on the return of form to emptiness;
second is the contemplation that emptiness is itself form.
Third, the contemplation of the non-obstruction between the three emptinesses and form;
fourth, the contemplation of total cessation and non-reliance.
The commentary states:
This is the listing of the names. Guan says:
Within the first gate, there are four [sections].
A single form is not identical to emptiness,
precisely because it is identical to emptiness. Why is this?
Because form is not identical to the emptiness of annihilation,
it is not [merely] empty;
because form, in its entirety, is true emptiness.
Therefore it is said: "Because it is identical with emptiness.
This is truly because it is identical with true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*), and thus it is not a nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*).
For this reason, it is said: "Because it is by virtue of being empty, it is not [merely] empty."
The commentary states:
Each of the four contemplations consists of three sections, namely:
the thesis, the explanation, and the conclusion.
However, according to the subsequent text, the first three [sections] distinguish the emotional mind from the Dharma,
while the fourth correctly reveals the principle of the Dharma to distinguish it from the emotional mind. Thus,
while the three phrases are identical in their designation of names, they differ in their explanation of the meanings.
Now, first, the three phrases that perform the exclusion will be explained in general.
There are three such exclusions:
first, the exclusion of identity and difference.
Second, the exclusion of distracted intention;
third, the exclusion of form and manifestation.
Regarding the first, speaking in terms of general characteristics, all three phrases serve as exclusions.
This refers to "separation" as spoken of in its predominant sense.
The first phrase clarifies that emptiness is not separate from form,
thereby distinguishing it from being separate from form.
The second phrase clarifies that emptiness is not identical to form,
thereby eliminating the extreme of total identity.
The third phrase clarifies both that they are neither identical nor separate.
"Discernment is itself detachment," because one discerns the three types of craving;
the fourth phrase reveals the correct principle.
Second, regarding the exclusion of confused intentions:
this refers to the *Ratnagotravibhāga*,
which clarifies that there are three types of confused intentions concerning emptiness for bodhisattvas prior to the [first] bhūmi.
Because they do not understand that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the equality of the two limits of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, they cling to three kinds of emptiness:
first, that it is empty because of annihilation.
The first phrase excludes [the internal];
the second takes the emptiness external to form;
the third phrase excludes [that].
The third refers to taking emptiness to be existent;
the second phrase excludes this.
Since it thus excludes these three types of incorrect emptiness, [the following applies].
The fourth phrase explains true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The third [phrase] distinguishes form from that which manifests. Some say:
The first phrase indicates that the substance of shape and color is empty, yet this is not a void of annihilation.
The second phrase reveals that visible form lacks substance and is empty of intrinsic nature.
The third phrase indicates that emptiness is the single essence of both the formless and the manifest.
The fourth phrase states: "Form and emptiness are non-dual; both are empty of emptiness.
The commentary says:
This third meaning may at first glance appear reasonable.
Because the second [type of perception] contains the words "blue" or "yellow," it is said to be the manifestation of color;
whereas the first and third lack such words for "blue" or "yellow."
This is because it would then be for the sake of form and color.
To explain it in this way is inconsistent with the detailed analysis; why?
Because of the [distinction between] one and three.
Why does it not mention shape, color, length, shortness, and so forth?
Second, why does it speak universally only of manifest color (*varṇa*)?
Why does it distinguish shape from manifest color by excluding the latter as being subject to annihilation?
Is it not permissible to select and sever [these aspects] through cessation?

Second, as for manifest color (*varṇa*), how can it be said that the characteristics of blue and yellow are not themselves the principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) regarding form and shape (*saṃsthāna*)?
Why then can it not be said that length, shortness, squareness, and roundness are not true emptiness?
Therefore, the third explanation is not satisfactory;
it is sufficient to exclude the previous two [explanations] alone to clearly manifest true emptiness.
As for the second passage in the text stating that blue and yellow are not true emptiness,
this is because the characteristics of manifest color are clearly evident and their features are prominent.
Furthermore, shape and form (saṃsthāna-rūpa) are conventional designations,
while manifest color (varṇa-rūpa) is substantial.
Substantial form is itself emptiness.
The examples and their forms and characteristics are likewise empty.
Thus, one knows that all three phrases encompass both form and manifestation, both of which are identical to emptiness.
Next, the text is formally explained.
Now, first:
the first sentence has three parts;
the first is the heading.
Next, what follows explains this by distinguishing it from the emptiness that is a mere negation of form and from the emptiness of annihilation.
Regarding the phrase "separated from form":
Space exists outside of form.
Outside of form, there are further two [aspects]:
first, clarifying space in contrast to form.
Just as when a wall occupies a space, that which is outside the wall is empty;
this third phrase distinguishes emptiness by excluding the two types of cessation of form.
That is to say, just as one must eliminate earth to remove it from a dug well and bring forth emptiness, so too must one eliminate form.
Now, this very point is being examined.
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"That which previously existed and subsequently ceases to exist."
This is precisely what constitutes annihilation.
Now, both non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles possess this notion of annihilation;
however, the annihilation of non-Buddhists reverts to the Great Void.
The followers of the Two Vehicles sever [defilements] and return to nirvana;
thus Master Zhao said:
"Nothing is a greater illusion than having a physical body."
Therefore, one extinguishes the body to return to non-exertion;
there is nothing more diligent than possessing wisdom.
Thus, one severs wisdom to dissolve into emptiness.
It is further said:
"Wisdom is like a mixture of poison;
the physical form is like shackles."
Therefore, they would reduce the body to ashes and extinguish wisdom, utterly annihilating everything without remainder.
If one were to claim that entering extinction is identical to the great void, this would be entirely the same as the non-Buddhist paths.
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
If the essence of the mind were to perish, it would not differ from the conceptual proliferation of the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists;
therefore, the present text states that it is "not simply empty through annihilation.
Next, [the text] proceeds by taking form as the basis for the argument.
The above has been explained by means of emptiness;
therefore, the three [virtues] are established through the following conclusion.
Within this, first, the conclusion is made by way of meaning.
Because it is precisely emptiness, it is not annihilation.
The following section concludes by establishing the title.
Wuanguan said:
"The two forms are not identical with emptiness,
because they are indeed identical with emptiness."
Why is this? Because the characteristics of blue and yellow are not the principle of true emptiness; therefore, it is said that they are "not identical to emptiness."
However, since blue and yellow have no intrinsic nature and are entirely empty, they are said to be "identical with emptiness.
This is because the emptiness that consists in the lack of intrinsic nature in blue and yellow is not itself identical to blue and yellow.
Therefore, it is said that they are not identical with emptiness.
The commentary states:
this also consists of a heading, an explanation, and a conclusion.
In this explanation, two types of deluded attachments are distinguished:
first, distinguishing against the extreme of identity,
because one hears that "form is emptiness" yet does not understand that its nature is empty.
Consequently, one grasps at the marks of form and takes them to be true emptiness;
therefore, it is necessary to discern this.
Thus it is said: "The marks of blue and yellow are not the principle of true emptiness."
This merely distinguishes [the practitioner] from ordinary people.
It is because those of small capacity do not reckon that form is itself emptiness.
Next, regarding the passage beginning with "then blue and yellow... and so forth.
Clarity, too, does not possess an intrinsic nature apart from its characteristics;
rather, it is precisely the absence of substantiality in blue, yellow, and so forth that constitutes true emptiness.
For this reason, the two [characteristics and clarity] appear to be mutually excluded.
This also excludes the Hīnayāna;
however, this is an instance of citing dharmas to exclude both [the Hīnayāna] and [subjective] clinging.
The subsequent clarification that [dharmas] are not separate is merely an instance of citing dharmas.
The second [type] also uses the preceding passage to exclude the mistaken notion [of emptiness].
Regarding the third type of emptiness, they take emptiness itself to be an existent entity;
they claim that there exists a distinct thing which constitutes the essence of emptiness.
Therefore, I shall now distinguish them.
Thus, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:
"There is non-duality and inexhaustibility"—this single phrase from the sūtra.
One uses "selection" (*jian*) to exclude the emptiness of a distracted mind;
one uses "existence" (*you*) to exclude the emptiness of annihilationism;
and one uses "non-duality" (*er-bu*) to exclude the emptiness that is distinct from form and light.
One does not select emptiness as being existent by means of non-exhaustion;
it is not that the substance of existence is utterly extinguished,
for now it shall not be exhausted.
This means that if emptiness were a functional entity, it would be subject to exhaustion and cessation;
if there were exhaustion and cessation, there would be arising.
However, the characteristic of the dharma of emptiness is neither arising nor ceasing.
How could there be existence?
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says:
"These dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness; they are neither produced nor extinguished," and so forth.
Furthermore, the characteristics of blue and yellow are not themselves true emptiness;
they must necessarily lack intrinsic nature.
How could one then take that which is empty to be existent?
The third section, from "Good" (*liáng*) downwards,
forms the conclusion by citing the emptiness of non-substantiality and concluding that it is not a form-characteristic (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
If clarity and emptiness are not existent, how could there be form?
Guanding said:
"The three forms are not identical to emptiness, yet they are identical to emptiness."
Why is this? Because form does not exist within emptiness, it is not identical to emptiness;
because form has no intrinsic substance, it is identical to emptiness.
This is truly because form is understood as returning to emptiness;
within emptiness, there can certainly be no form.
Therefore, because form is empty, form itself is not empty.
The first three lines have completed the selection [of the true] Dharma from [deluded] sentiment.
The commentary states:
Within this section, there are two parts.
First, I shall explain the current phrase;
afterwards, I shall conclude by summarizing the preceding three. Within the former [section], there are also three parts.
First, the heading;
second, the explanation.
Within the explanation, one first uses a double negation to exclude both identity and difference.
Because there is no form within emptiness, form is not identical to emptiness;
because there is no such thing as emptiness apart from form, emptiness does not exclude form.
Only that which is neither identical nor separate constitutes true emptiness.
Second, distinguishing the distracted mind from the emptiness that is distinct from form:
they cling to the notion that there is an emptiness external to form that is different from form.
This is as previously explained regarding the elucidation of emptiness in contrast to form.
Now, it is clear that even within emptiness there is no form;
how, then, could there be an emptiness that stands in opposition to form?
Furthermore, because one realizes that form has no intrinsic substance, it is said to be identical with emptiness.
How could there be an emptiness that exists apart from form to stand in opposition to it?
As the ancients said:
"When form departs, emptiness does not remain."
Space does not abide in having a limit.
This concludes the preceding meaning by means of the three excellent [reasons] from below.
The following section concludes that [form] is not identical with emptiness;
it specifically establishes that by realizing form as emptiness, how could there be form within emptiness?
The two "upward" and three "downward" [sections] summarize the three gates.
The contemplation states:
"The four form-aggregates are themselves emptiness."
Why is this? Because all dharmas of form are necessarily not different from true emptiness,
for all dharmas of form are necessarily devoid of intrinsic nature.
Therefore, form is itself the cause.
Just as it is with the emptiness of form, so it is with all phenomena; reflect upon this.
The commentary states:
Within this, there are two parts.
First, the correct elucidation of the meaning of true emptiness; second, the conclusion that illustrates all phenomena by analogy.
The preceding section also has three parts:
first, the heading;
second, the explanation.
Regarding the statement "because form follows conditions and necessarily lacks intrinsic nature":
the absence of intrinsic nature in the dependent nature is itself the true emptiness of the perfected nature.
This concludes the preceding three points.
Since it is neither the cessation of form nor something different from form—
being neither identical with nor separate from it— it is thus true emptiness.
Emptiness is not the characteristic of form, for there is no pervasive conceptual construction.
Dependent origination being without intrinsic nature is precisely the absence of nature in the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
This truth of the absence of nature is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Therefore, this true emptiness thoroughly penetrates both essence and appearance.
"Second, 'As it is with the emptiness of form,' and so forth," concludes by applying this analogy to all phenomena;
whereas the preceding four gates merely clarified the emptiness of form.
Form (*rūpa*) is the foremost of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*),
as it is the first of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Thus, whenever the various sūtras and śāstras expound upon a single principle...
This is because they all first take form (rūpa) as their basis.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other scriptures,
there are over eighty sections ranging from form up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
All these cases take form as the paradigm;
now this case is likewise used as a paradigm for all phenomena.
To summarize briefly, no phenomenon falls outside the ten pairs mentioned above; regarding their underlying substance and basis, there is nothing that is not itself emptiness.
In all cases, one must use the Dharma to discern and transcend emotional attachments,
thereby manifesting that phenomena return to the ultimate principle.
The *Vipaśyanā* says:
The second explains the contemplation of emptiness as being identical to form;
herein, it is also treated according to four sections.
The commentary states:
This is the general heading.
However, the general characteristics of these four gates merely reverse the preceding four;
likewise, the first three phrases use dharmas to distinguish them from mental states.
The fourth phrase correctly reveals the principle of the Dharma.
Within the context of distinguishing it from the realm of ordinary sentiment, its meaning is largely identical to the preceding discussion on the emptiness of form.
The wording is slightly different,
yet the headings are the same; however, there are distinctions in the explanations of their meanings.
Now, first, there is a general selection,
which also has three meanings.
The first is the selection of identity and difference.
Second, distinguishing from a distracted mind;
third, distinguishing from form and manifestation.
Regarding the first [of these], the first phrase clarifies that true emptiness is not separate from the preceding form.
The second phrase clarifies that true emptiness is not identical with the characteristics of form.
The third phrase clarifies that true emptiness is a double negation—neither identical with nor separate from form.
The second [section] distinguishes against three types of confused interpretations.
The first phrase clarifies that the emptiness resulting from cessation is not substantial form.
The second phrase clarifies that the existence of characteristics is not true emptiness; this serves to distinguish it from the existence of characteristics.
The third phrase clarifies that the basis is not the dependent,
thereby excluding the dependent;
its third meaning excludes those that are shape-based rather than color-based.
Some say: "The first phrase clarifies that non-annihilating emptiness does not obstruct form-color (*rūpa-varṇa*);
the second phrase clarifies that intrinsic-nature emptiness does not obstruct manifest-color (*saṃsthāna-varṇa*)."
The third phrase clarifies that within the single essence of emptiness, both [emptiness and form] do not obstruct one another;
the fourth phrase clarifies that within the emptiness of both, emptiness does not obstruct the two—emptiness and form.
The explanation states:
The previous contemplation on the reduction of form to emptiness has already been discussed.
